item.content:encoded:
The Government of Ireland’s Civil Society Fund 2027 is now open, offering substantial grant funding to eligible civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects. Through the fund, the Department of Foreign Affairs can provide up to 100% of eligible annual project costs, with grants of up to €800,000 per year for projects lasting as long as five years.

The Civil Society Fund is designed to support development interventions delivered by civil society organisations and aligned with Ireland’s international development priorities. The programme also recognises the importance of sustained responses to long-term humanitarian crises, although sudden-onset acute emergency responses are not eligible.

The 2027 call involves a two-stage application process. Organisations must first establish their eligibility and, if eligible, will subsequently receive the full application form. Irish-based organisations that believe they meet the requirements are required to submit an Eligibility Form by 5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026. Eligible organisations will then be invited to submit the full application by 5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026.

Ireland Civil Society Fund 2027 at a Glance

Opportunity Details
Programme Civil Society Fund 2027
Funder Government of Ireland / Department of Foreign Affairs
Implementing department Development Cooperation and Africa Division
Opportunity type Overseas development grant
Maximum funding Up to €800,000 per annum
Maximum project duration Up to five years
Funding level Up to 100% of annual project costs for successful applications
Eligible applicants Irish civil society organisations and specifically invited international civil society organisations
Application structure Eligibility Form followed by full application for eligible organisations
Initial eligibility deadline 5pm, Friday, 11 September 2026
Full application deadline 5pm, Monday, 2 November 2026
Eligibility notification Late September 2026
Appraisal period December 2026/January 2027
Funding decisions March/April 2027
Project focus Overseas development projects
Long-term humanitarian crises Eligible
Sudden-onset acute emergency responses Not eligible

What Is the Civil Society Fund?

The Civil Society Fund (CSF) is a funding mechanism through which the Government of Ireland supports civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects.

The fund provides financial support for organisations undertaking development work outside Ireland and is intended for interventions that contribute to international development objectives.

Rather than being an individual funding opportunity, this is an organisational grant programme. Applications are submitted by qualifying civil society organisations rather than individuals.

For successful applicants, the Department can fund up to 100% of annual project costs, subject to the applicable grant ceiling and other requirements.

The maximum grant available is €800,000 per annum, while projects can have a duration of up to five years.

This means that organisations selected for multi-year support could potentially receive significant funding over the life of a project, although the exact amount awarded will depend on the approved project, annual costs, funding conditions and assessment process.

What Does the Civil Society Fund Support?

The fund is intended to support overseas development projects implemented by eligible civil society organisations.

The programme is therefore particularly relevant to organisations that already have the capacity, experience and institutional structures necessary to design and implement development interventions outside Ireland.

Potential applicant organisations should carefully examine the official 2027 Call for Applications to determine whether their proposed intervention fits within the fund’s specific policy priorities, geographic requirements and thematic criteria.

The fund is not simply a general-purpose organisational funding programme. Applicants must propose eligible development interventions and satisfy the requirements established in the official call.

Up to €800,000 Per Year in Grant Funding

One of the most significant features of the Civil Society Fund is its maximum funding level.

Successful applicants can receive:

Up to €800,000 per year

The fund can also support projects lasting:

Up to five years

The Department states that, for successful applications, it will fund up to 100% of annual project costs, up to the maximum grant limit.

This can provide eligible civil society organisations with substantial resources to implement development programmes over an extended period.

However, organisations should not interpret the €800,000 figure as an automatic award. It is the maximum available grant per annum, and funding decisions will depend on the quality, relevance, eligibility and assessment of each application.

Important Organisational Income Requirement

Applicants should pay particular attention to the Civil Society Fund’s organisational income requirement.

Income received from the Department, whether directly or indirectly, must not exceed 49% of the applicant organisation’s overall income.

The calculation is based on an average of the organisation’s published audited accounts over the previous three years.

Importantly, in-kind income is excluded from this calculation.

This requirement means organisations should review their financial records before proceeding with an application.

An organisation that relies too heavily on income from the Department of Foreign Affairs may not satisfy this particular eligibility requirement.

Applicants should therefore examine their audited accounts for the relevant three-year period and calculate the proportion of overall organisational income originating directly or indirectly from the Department.

Long-Term Humanitarian Crises Are Eligible

The Civil Society Fund makes an important distinction between long-term humanitarian crises and sudden-onset emergencies.

Interventions addressing long-term humanitarian crises can be eligible for support.

This creates an opportunity for organisations working on sustained humanitarian challenges where development and humanitarian needs persist over an extended period.

However, the fund does not support responses to sudden-onset acute emergencies.

Therefore, organisations proposing projects should distinguish clearly between:

  • Long-term humanitarian crises requiring sustained interventions; and
  • Sudden-onset emergencies requiring immediate emergency response.

A proposal focused primarily on responding to a newly occurring acute emergency would not meet this aspect of the fund’s eligibility.

Who Can Apply?

The Civil Society Fund is primarily open to Irish civil society organisations that meet the eligibility criteria set out in the 2027 Call for Applications.

The opportunity also allows for participation by a limited number of international civil society organisations, but there is an important restriction.

International organisations cannot simply apply independently because they discover the call.

The Government states that a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited to the Civil Society Fund each year, based on policy priorities.

Therefore:

  • Irish-based civil society organisations that meet the requirements can proceed through the published eligibility process.
  • International civil society organisations are eligible only if specifically invited.
  • An international organisation that has not been invited should not assume that it can submit an application.

This distinction is particularly important for NGOs and development organisations based in Africa, Asia, Latin America and other regions.

Can African NGOs Apply?

African civil society organisations should not assume that the Civil Society Fund is an open global grant competition.

The official information specifically states that a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited each year.

Therefore, an African NGO, for example, would need to determine whether it has been specifically invited to participate in the 2027 Civil Society Fund.

Being an NGO, having a strong development project or operating in a country relevant to international development does not, by itself, establish eligibility under the international-organisation provision.

Potential international applicants should consult the official 2027 Call for Applications and use the contact details provided by the Department if they need clarification.

Eligibility Is the First Stage

The Civil Society Fund uses a staged application process.

Organisations do not immediately submit the full grant application.

Instead, eligible Irish-based organisations begin by completing an Eligibility Form.

This first stage allows the Department to determine whether the organisation meets the basic requirements before inviting it to submit the full application.

This means organisations should treat the Eligibility Form as an important part of the application process rather than as a simple registration exercise.

First Deadline: Eligibility Form

Irish organisations that intend to apply must submit their completed Eligibility Form to the Civil Society Fund mailbox by:

5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026

This is the first major deadline.

Organisations should not wait until the final day because they need to gather supporting documents and ensure that the submission is complete.

The Department specifically requests that applicants also provide supporting documentation, including:

  • A Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent
  • Accounts for the last three years
  • Relevant safeguarding policies

The Eligibility Form and supporting documents should therefore be prepared together.

What Happens After the Eligibility Form?

Organisations that submit a completed Eligibility Form will be notified about their eligibility in late September 2026.

Organisations determined to be eligible will then receive the full application form by email.

This creates a two-stage process:

Stage 1: Eligibility

Submit:

  • Completed Eligibility Form
  • Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent
  • Three years of accounts
  • Safeguarding policies

Deadline: 5pm, 11 September 2026

Stage 2: Full Grant Application

If the organisation is confirmed as eligible, the Department will email the full application form.

The completed application must then be submitted by:

5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026

Applicants should understand that submitting the Eligibility Form does not automatically mean that the organisation will be invited to submit a full proposal. The organisation must first be assessed as eligible.

Second Deadline: Full Application

The full application deadline is:

5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026

The Department states that applications received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.

Organisations should therefore plan backwards from the deadline and leave sufficient time for:

  • Internal review
  • Financial verification
  • Safeguarding review
  • Senior management approval
  • Legal review where necessary
  • Final editing
  • Submission
  • Printing and signing of the required hard copy

Hard Copy Submission Requirement

The application process also includes a subsequent hard-copy submission.

After submitting the application form, applicants must submit a hard copy of the application form, signed by the legal representative of the organisation.

The hard copy should be sent to:

Civil Society Fund
Civil Society Unit
Development Cooperation and Africa Division
Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade
Riverstone House
23–27 Henry Street
Limerick
V94 R7YE
Ireland

Organisations should therefore allow sufficient time for the physical document to reach the Department after completing the electronic application requirements.

Safeguarding Requirements

Safeguarding is an important component of the eligibility documentation.

Applicants are required to provide their safeguarding policies alongside the Eligibility Form.

This is particularly relevant because organisations receiving development funding may work directly with:

  • Children
  • Women and girls
  • People experiencing poverty
  • Displaced populations
  • Refugees
  • People with disabilities
  • Communities affected by conflict
  • Other vulnerable or marginalised groups

Organisations should ensure that their safeguarding policies are current, formally approved and appropriate to the nature of their proposed development work.

Financial Documentation

Applicants must also provide accounts covering the last three years.

These documents are important for demonstrating the organisation’s financial position and for assessing compliance with the Civil Society Fund’s income requirements.

Organisations should ensure that their accounts are:

  • Complete
  • Published or formally audited where required
  • Consistent across the relevant three-year period
  • Readily available for submission
  • Compatible with the information provided in the Eligibility Form

Financial information should be carefully checked before submission because discrepancies between the eligibility form and financial statements could create problems during assessment.

Tax Clearance

Applicants must include a Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent with their eligibility submission.

This is another indication that the fund is designed for established organisations with appropriate financial and legal structures.

Organisations should verify that their tax documentation is valid and meets the Department’s requirements before submitting the Eligibility Form.

Application Assessment Timeline

Following the application process, the Department intends to assess applications during:

December 2026 and January 2027

Funding decisions are expected to be communicated in:

March/April 2027

The timeline therefore provides applicants with several months between the full application deadline and the expected funding decision.

However, organisations should not assume that funding will be available before the official notification of a decision.

Important Application Rules

Applicants should pay close attention to the Department’s procedural requirements.

Late applications are not accepted

The Department states that forms received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.

This applies to the relevant stages of the process, so applicants should submit their documents before the stated closing times.

Individual meetings are not available

Once the Call for Applications is issued, representatives of applicant organisations cannot request individual meetings concerning the application form until funding decisions have been communicated.

This means organisations should rely on the official documentation and the designated Civil Society Fund contact channel for questions.

Attempts to influence the decision can lead to disqualification

The Department explicitly states that any attempt to influence the outcome of the decision-making process in relation to grant applications will result in disqualification.

Applicants should therefore maintain a professional and transparent application process and avoid inappropriate attempts to influence officials or the assessment process.

Organisations based in Ireland that consider they meet the criteria set out in the 2027 Call for Applications and who wish to apply for funding can download an Eligibility Form.

How Organisations Should Prepare

Although applicants should rely on the official call for the complete requirements, organisations can begin preparing immediately.

1. Review the eligibility requirements

Start by reading the full 2027 Call for Applications carefully.

Do not begin with the project narrative before confirming that the organisation itself is eligible.

2. Review three years of financial records

Check the organisation’s published audited accounts for the relevant three-year period.

Calculate the proportion of organisational income received directly or indirectly from the Department to determine whether the organisation satisfies the 49% income requirement.

3. Prepare safeguarding documentation

Make sure safeguarding policies are current and can be provided with the Eligibility Form.

4. Confirm tax clearance

Obtain the relevant Tax Clearance Certificate or equivalent documentation.

5. Examine the proposed development project

The project should clearly correspond to the objectives and eligibility requirements of the Civil Society Fund.

Organisations should be able to explain:

  • What development problem they are addressing
  • Where the project will operate
  • Who will benefit
  • Why the intervention is necessary
  • What outcomes are expected
  • How activities will produce those outcomes
  • How progress will be measured
  • How the intervention will be sustained
  • How risks will be managed
  • Why the organisation is appropriately positioned to implement it

6. Build a realistic budget

Because funding can cover up to 100% of annual project costs for successful applications, organisations should prepare a realistic and well-supported project budget.

The budget should correspond directly with the activities and expected results of the project.

7. Plan for a multi-year intervention where appropriate

Projects can last for up to five years.

Organisations with interventions requiring sustained implementation should consider how activities, outcomes, partnerships and financing would develop over the full project period.

8. Begin internal approvals early

The application may require approval from senior management, a board, legal representatives or other authorised personnel.

Organisations should therefore avoid leaving internal approval until the final days before submission.

Why the Civil Society Fund Is Significant

The scale and duration of the Civil Society Fund make it potentially valuable for established development organisations.

A maximum annual grant of €800,000 provides considerably more funding capacity than many small community or seed grants.

The possibility of funding projects for up to five years also makes the programme relevant to interventions that require long-term implementation rather than short-term activities.

Longer-term development programmes may involve:

  • Institutional strengthening
  • Community development
  • Capacity building
  • Education
  • Health
  • Gender equality
  • Poverty reduction
  • Governance
  • Human rights
  • Livelihood development
  • Resilience building
  • Long-term humanitarian support

However, the specific thematic and geographic priorities of the 2027 call should always be checked before preparing a proposal.

Important Distinction: Grant Funding vs Individual Funding

This opportunity is a grant for civil society organisations, not an individual scholarship or fellowship.

Individuals cannot apply for the €800,000 grant as individuals.

Similarly, students, job seekers and individual researchers should not treat the Civil Society Fund as a personal funding programme.

The applicant is the eligible organisation, which must demonstrate the institutional, financial, legal and safeguarding capacity required by the programme.

What International Organisations Should Know

International civil society organisations should pay particular attention to the invitation requirement.

The Government of Ireland states that only a limited number of international civil society organisations may be invited each year.

Eligibility is determined according to policy priorities, and only organisations specifically invited are eligible to apply.

Therefore, international NGOs should not assume that the publication of the call means that every international organisation worldwide can submit an application.

This is especially important for organisations headquartered outside Ireland.

Geographic Eligibility

The Civil Society Fund supports overseas development projects, meaning the programme is relevant to development activities implemented outside Ireland.

The official page also provides an OECD DAC Country Codes / ODA recipients resource as one of the key documents for the call.

Organisations should consult the official 2027 Call for Applications and the OECD DAC list to determine whether their proposed project location meets the relevant development-assistance requirements.

For African organisations, geographic relevance should therefore be assessed alongside the separate requirement concerning whether an international organisation has been specifically invited.

Key Documents

Applicants should review the official programme documents before preparing their submission.

The key documents include:

  • 2027 Call for Applications
  • OECD DAC Country Codes / ODA Recipient List
  • 2027 Civil Society Fund Eligibility Form

The official Civil Society Fund webpage also provides access to these documents and additional programme information.

Application Deadlines

There are two critical deadlines for the 2027 Civil Society Fund.

Eligibility Form

5pm, Friday, 11 September 2026

This is the deadline for eligible Irish-based organisations to submit the completed Eligibility Form and required supporting documents.

Full Application

5pm, Monday, 2 November 2026

Only organisations that are confirmed as eligible will receive the full application form and proceed to this stage.

Organisations should not confuse the two deadlines. The 11 September 2026 deadline is the first-stage eligibility deadline, while 2 November 2026 is the deadline for the full application.

Key Takeaways for Prospective Applicants

Before applying, organisations should remember the following:

  1. The Civil Society Fund supports overseas development projects.
  2. It is an organisational grant, not an individual funding opportunity.
  3. Successful projects can receive up to €800,000 per year.
  4. Projects can run for up to five years.
  5. The Department can fund up to 100% of annual project costs, subject to the grant limit and applicable conditions.
  6. Departmental income must not exceed 49% of the applicant organisation’s overall income, calculated using the average of published audited accounts over three years.
  7. Long-term humanitarian crisis interventions are eligible.
  8. Sudden-onset acute emergency responses are not eligible.
  9. Irish civil society organisations can apply if they meet the requirements.
  10. International civil society organisations must be specifically invited to apply.
  11. The first stage requires an Eligibility Form.
  12. Applicants must provide financial accounts, tax clearance documentation and safeguarding policies.
  13. The Eligibility Form deadline is 5pm, 11 September 2026.
  14. Eligible organisations will be notified in late September 2026.
  15. The full application deadline is 5pm, 2 November 2026.
  16. Applications received after the relevant deadlines will not be considered.
  17. Appraisal is expected in December 2026/January 2027.
  18. Funding decisions are expected in March/April 2027.
  19. A signed hard copy of the application must subsequently be submitted to the Civil Society Fund in Limerick.
  20. Attempts to influence the funding decision can result in disqualification.

Conclusion

The Ireland Civil Society Fund 2027 represents a significant funding opportunity for eligible civil society organisations implementing overseas development projects. With grants of up to €800,000 per annum, the possibility of projects lasting up to five years, and funding of up to 100% of annual project costs, the programme can provide substantial support for well-designed and strategically relevant development interventions.

However, organisations should pay close attention to the eligibility conditions. The opportunity is primarily available to Irish civil society organisations, while only a limited number of international civil society organisations specifically invited by the Government of Ireland may apply. It is therefore not an open global grant competition for every NGO.

The application process has two important stages. Irish organisations intending to apply must first submit the Eligibility Form and required documentation by 5pm on Friday, 11 September 2026. Organisations that are confirmed as eligible will receive the full application form and must submit it by 5pm on Monday, 2 November 2026.

Prospective applicants should begin preparations early by reviewing the official call, checking their financial eligibility, preparing their three years of accounts, confirming tax clearance, reviewing safeguarding policies and developing a strong project concept aligned with the fund’s requirements.

The Civil Society Fund can be particularly valuable for established organisations seeking substantial, multi-year support for overseas development work, but applicants should carefully verify all eligibility, thematic, geographic and financial requirements in the official 2027 Call for Applications before submitting.

Government of Ireland – Civil Society Fund 2027

item.content:encoded:
The Lisbon AI Safety Hub (LAISH) is inviting students and working professionals to apply for its Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship, an eight-week programme designed to introduce participants to the rapidly developing field of artificial intelligence safety and help them identify meaningful ways to contribute to the safe development and governance of advanced AI.

Based in Lisbon, Portugal, the Lisbon AI Safety Hub is building a community that brings together researchers, academics, policymakers and ambitious individuals who want to contribute to the development of safe and responsibly governed artificial intelligence.

The fellowship provides an opportunity for participants who may not have a technical background in artificial intelligence to understand the opportunities and risks associated with increasingly capable AI systems. Through the programme, participants will explore AI safety, understand major risks associated with advanced AI, examine governance approaches and consider practical career and professional pathways through which they can contribute to the field.

Applications for the current fellowship cohort opened on August 1, with applications closing on September 30. The cohort is scheduled to begin on October 6.

About the Lisbon AI Safety Hub

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub is a community-focused organisation working to help Portugal play a meaningful role in the development of advanced artificial intelligence and the emerging global AI safety field.

The organisation brings together people from different professional and academic backgrounds, including:

  • Researchers
  • Academics
  • Policymakers
  • Students
  • Technology professionals
  • Individuals interested in AI safety and governance
  • People looking for ways to contribute to the responsible development of advanced AI

LAISH takes a broad view of AI safety. Rather than treating the subject purely as a technical computer science problem, the organisation describes AI safety as a sociotechnical problem, meaning that technical research, governance, institutions, policy and human decision-making all have important roles to play.

Its goal is to help develop a community capable of contributing to safer AI development in Portugal and beyond.

What Is AI Safety?

Artificial intelligence systems are becoming increasingly capable and are being integrated into more areas of society, business, research and government.

As AI capabilities increase, an important question arises: how can humans ensure that increasingly powerful AI systems remain aligned with human intentions, values and interests?

AI safety broadly concerns the research, policies, institutions and practices needed to reduce the risks associated with advanced artificial intelligence.

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub highlights three major areas of AI safety:

1. AI Alignment

AI alignment focuses on ensuring that advanced AI systems pursue objectives that reflect what humans actually intend.

A system may technically follow an instruction while still producing an outcome that humans did not want. Alignment research therefore examines how AI systems can better understand and follow human goals and intentions as their capabilities become more powerful.

The fellowship introduces participants to the importance of alignment and the challenges involved in ensuring that increasingly capable systems remain under meaningful human direction.

2. AI Interpretability

Interpretability focuses on understanding what is happening inside AI systems.

Modern neural networks can be extremely complex, making it difficult for humans to understand precisely how they arrive at particular decisions or outputs.

Interpretability research seeks to make these systems more understandable so researchers can potentially:

  • Identify what AI systems have learned
  • Understand how systems represent information
  • Detect potential problems
  • Predict certain types of failure
  • Audit AI behaviour
  • Intervene before problems become more serious

Understanding how AI systems work internally is therefore an important part of developing safer and more reliable systems.

3. AI Governance

AI governance concerns the rules, policies, institutions and international arrangements that influence how powerful AI systems are developed and deployed.

Governance questions include:

  • Who should be allowed to develop frontier AI?
  • What safeguards should developers follow?
  • What limits should apply to advanced AI systems?
  • How should governments regulate powerful AI technologies?
  • Who should be held accountable when AI systems cause harm?
  • How can countries cooperate on AI safety?
  • What institutions are needed to manage increasingly capable AI?

The governance side of AI safety provides opportunities for people with backgrounds in areas such as public policy, law, international relations, economics, governance, communications and social sciences.

About the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship is a non-technical programme designed to give participants an introduction to AI risks and practical ways they can contribute to efforts to make advanced AI safer.

Importantly, participants do not need prior technical knowledge to apply.

The programme is structured to help participants progress from understanding the fundamental AI safety problem to considering how they personally might contribute.

The fellowship covers four main areas.

1. Why AI Safety Matters

Participants begin by developing an understanding of advanced artificial intelligence and why AI safety has become an increasingly important area of work.

This includes exploring:

  • The development of increasingly capable AI systems
  • The potential benefits of advanced AI
  • Potential risks associated with advanced AI
  • Why AI safety is becoming increasingly important
  • Why maintaining meaningful human control over powerful AI systems matters

The aim is to provide participants with a foundation for understanding why AI safety is considered an important emerging field.

2. Understanding the Risks

The fellowship then examines the different ways advanced artificial intelligence could affect individuals, institutions and society.

Participants explore major categories of AI risk and learn how people working in the field think about and evaluate those risks.

This part of the fellowship can help participants develop a more structured understanding of questions surrounding:

  • AI reliability
  • AI alignment
  • AI system behaviour
  • Societal impacts
  • Risks associated with increasingly capable systems
  • Potential failure modes
  • The challenges of managing advanced AI

Rather than requiring participants to already be experts, the programme provides an introductory pathway into these discussions.

3. Governance and Action

Another major component of the fellowship focuses on governance.

Participants examine how policy, institutions and international coordination can contribute to safer AI development.

This is particularly relevant for individuals interested in careers involving:

  • Public policy
  • Technology policy
  • Government
  • International affairs
  • Regulation
  • Research
  • Governance
  • Responsible technology
  • AI policy
  • Institutional decision-making

The governance component demonstrates that contributing to AI safety does not necessarily require becoming an AI engineer or machine-learning researcher.

4. Identifying Your Next Step

The final component focuses on helping participants identify practical ways to contribute to AI safety.

Participants are encouraged to consider how their existing skills, education, professional experience and interests could connect with opportunities in the field.

Possible pathways may include:

  • Career development
  • Academic research
  • Policy work
  • Governance
  • Technical research
  • Community building
  • Communications
  • Advocacy
  • Further study
  • Work related to responsible AI

This makes the fellowship relevant not only to people who are already working in artificial intelligence, but also to people considering a transition into the field.

Fellowship Duration, Location and Important Dates

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship has the following programme details:

Programme: Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship

Duration: 8 weeks

Location: Lisbon, Portugal

Format: In person

Applications opened: August 1

Application deadline: September 30

Cohort starts: October 6

Target participants: Students and working professionals

Technical prerequisites: No technical knowledge required

Applicants should take note of the September 30 application deadline and submit their applications before the closing date.

Who Should Apply?

The fellowship is particularly relevant to students and working professionals who want to learn more about artificial intelligence safety and explore ways to contribute to the field.

You may be a suitable candidate if you are:

A student interested in AI

Students who are curious about artificial intelligence, technology, research, policy or the societal effects of AI can use the fellowship to develop a foundational understanding of AI safety.

The programme may also help students identify potential areas for further study or career development.

A working professional considering a career transition

Professionals from fields outside traditional artificial intelligence can explore how their existing skills could be applied to AI safety.

For example, people with experience in policy, communications, research, governance, law, management, technology or other professional areas may find the programme useful.

Someone interested in AI governance

People interested in the rules and institutions surrounding artificial intelligence may particularly benefit from the governance component of the programme.

This can be relevant to individuals interested in government, public policy, regulation, international cooperation and technology governance.

Someone without a technical AI background

One of the important features of the programme is that no technical knowledge is required.

This means that applicants should not assume they need to be programmers, machine-learning engineers or AI researchers before they can participate.

The fellowship is designed to provide an introduction to the field and help participants understand where their own skills and interests could fit.

Why the Fellowship Is Important

Artificial intelligence is developing rapidly, and increasingly capable systems are expected to influence many areas of society.

This creates a growing need for people who can think about AI not only from a technical perspective but also from the perspectives of governance, policy, institutions and society.

A field such as AI safety therefore requires people with different backgrounds and skill sets.

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub’s approach recognises this by supporting both technical and governance-oriented work.

This broad perspective means that someone does not necessarily have to become a machine-learning researcher to contribute to AI safety.

Instead, individuals may contribute through:

  • Technical research
  • Policy development
  • Governance
  • Regulation
  • Academic research
  • Institutional design
  • Communications
  • Community building
  • International coordination
  • Other professional areas connected to responsible AI development

Other Ways to Get Involved With the Lisbon AI Safety Hub

The fellowship is only one of several ways to engage with the Lisbon AI Safety Hub.

Events and Lectures

LAISH organises events designed to help grow the AI safety community.

These include:

  • Film screenings
  • Directed discussion groups
  • Community meetings
  • Lectures from industry experts
  • Research discussions
  • Social events

The organisation states that events are primarily held in English, although Portuguese speakers are expected to be present.

Career Guidance

LAISH also offers career guidance for individuals interested in working in AI safety.

Participants can seek tailored advice about opportunities in the field and ways to develop a career that enables them to contribute to AI safety.

This can be useful for people who understand that they are interested in the field but are unsure which professional or academic direction to take.

Click HERE for more information.

Newsletter

The organisation publishes a newsletter covering topics such as:

  • Frontier AI news
  • Jobs
  • Fellowships
  • Opportunities within the AI safety field

The newsletter is available in English and Portuguese.

Community Discord

LAISH also maintains a Discord community where people can connect with other members, exchange resources and receive information about events and community activities.

This provides an additional way for people to remain connected to the AI safety community beyond individual programmes.

What Makes This Fellowship Different?

One of the strongest features of the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship is its accessibility to people without technical AI expertise.

Many emerging technology programmes focus heavily on programming, mathematics, machine learning or computer science.

The Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship instead provides an introductory pathway that allows participants to understand the broader AI safety landscape before deciding how they might contribute.

The programme combines:

  1. Understanding advanced AI
  2. Exploring AI risks
  3. Learning about AI governance
  4. Considering practical career pathways

This makes it potentially valuable for people coming from different educational and professional backgrounds.

Potential Career Directions After Learning About AI Safety

Although participation in the fellowship does not automatically qualify someone for a particular job, developing knowledge of AI safety can help participants explore several career directions.

Depending on their existing background and future training, participants may consider areas such as:

  • AI policy
  • Technology governance
  • AI safety research
  • AI governance research
  • Public policy
  • Responsible AI
  • AI regulation
  • Academic research
  • Technology communications
  • AI-related programme management
  • International AI policy
  • Community development

Participants can also use the fellowship to determine whether they want to pursue more specialised technical or governance training.

APPLY HERE.

How to Apply

Interested applicants should apply through the Lisbon AI Safety Hub’s official fellowship application process.

Applications for the current cohort opened on August 1 and close on September 30.

The programme begins on October 6 and lasts for eight weeks.

Because the fellowship is listed as an in-person programme in Lisbon, applicants should carefully consider their ability to participate in the programme at the stated location.

Applicants who have questions can contact the Lisbon AI Safety Hub at:

contact@lisbonaisafetyhub.org

Important Details at a Glance

  • Opportunity: Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship
  • Organisation: Lisbon AI Safety Hub (LAISH)
  • Location: Lisbon, Portugal
  • Programme format: In person
  • Duration: 8 weeks
  • Application opening date: August 1
  • Application deadline: September 30
  • Cohort start date: October 6
  • Who can apply: Students and working professionals
  • Technical knowledge required: No
  • Main areas: AI safety, AI risks, alignment, interpretability and governance
  • Career focus: Identifying practical ways to contribute to AI safety

Is the Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship a scholarship?

No. Based on the information provided, this is a fellowship programme, not a scholarship.

The provided information does not state that participants receive tuition funding, a stipend, travel support or other financial benefits. Applicants should therefore avoid assuming that the programme is fully funded unless LAISH confirms otherwise.

Do I need to know programming to apply?

No.

Who is the fellowship for?

The programme is intended for students and working professionals who want to learn about AI safety and explore ways of contributing to the field.

Do I need an AI degree?

No specific AI degree is listed as a prerequisite.

The programme is designed as an introduction to AI safety and does not require technical knowledge.

Is the fellowship online?

The fellowship is listed as in person in Lisbon, Portugal.

Therefore, applicants should be prepared to participate physically in Lisbon.

When does the application close?

The application deadline is September 30.

When does the cohort begin?

The cohort is scheduled to begin on October 6.

How long does the fellowship last?

The programme lasts eight weeks.

Can people from outside Portugal apply?

No. The fellowship explicitly states that no technical knowledge is required.

What areas of AI safety are covered?

The programme introduces participants to why AI safety matters, the risks associated with advanced AI, governance and practical ways to contribute.

The wider LAISH approach also highlights areas including alignment, interpretability and governance.

Conclusion

The Lisbon AI Safety Hub Foundations of AI Safety Fellowship provides an accessible entry point into one of the world’s emerging technology fields.

As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly capable, questions about how these systems can remain safe, reliable and subject to meaningful human direction are becoming increasingly important. Addressing these questions requires more than technical expertise alone. It also requires people who understand policy, governance, institutions, research, communication and the broader societal implications of AI.

With its eight-week, in-person programme in Lisbon, the fellowship offers students and working professionals an opportunity to develop foundational knowledge of AI safety, explore the risks associated with advanced AI, understand governance approaches and consider practical ways to contribute to the field.

The fact that no technical knowledge is required makes the programme particularly accessible to people who are interested in AI safety but do not come from a computer science or engineering background.

For individuals interested in the future of artificial intelligence and the challenge of ensuring that increasingly powerful AI remains beneficial and responsibly governed, the programme could provide an important starting point.

item.content:encoded:
Highly technical students and recent software engineering graduates looking for an opportunity to accelerate their careers in the startup ecosystem can apply for the Alpha Fellowship, a programme designed to place exceptional early-career engineers into full-time roles at fast-growing companies within the Andreessen Horowitz ecosystem or provide aspiring founders with capital to begin building their own company.

The Alpha Fellowship is designed for ambitious technical builders who do not want to wait years before taking on meaningful responsibility.

Participants can follow one of two pathways. The Startup Track connects successful fellows with fast-growing portfolio companies for full-time engineering positions that include salary and equity. The Founder Track is designed for individuals who want to build their own startup and provides early capital even when they do not yet have a formal company, established team or fully developed idea.

Both pathways begin with an approximately two-month, eight-week, in-person fellowship experience that includes an immersive retreat, founder discussions, curated dinners, small-group conversations and opportunities to interact with engineers, startup founders, operators and investors.

The programme also provides fellows with access to the broader a16z speedrun and EO Ventures communities and events.

For applicants who want to work at a rapidly growing technology company, become a founder or gain exposure to experienced entrepreneurs and investors, Alpha offers a potentially significant early-career pathway.

What Is the Alpha Fellowship?

The Alpha Fellowship is an early-career programme focused on highly technical software engineers who have demonstrated an ability and desire to build.

Its central proposition is straightforward: rather than waiting for an opportunity to emerge, technically strong students and recent graduates can use Alpha as a direct route into either a high-growth startup or entrepreneurship.

The programme offers two main choices:

  1. Join a breakout portfolio company through the Startup Track.
  2. Start your own company through the Founder Track.

The fellowship component provides an intensive in-person experience, while the two tracks provide different long-term outcomes.

For Startup Track participants, the fellowship is combined with a full-time engineering position.

For Founder Track participants, the fellowship is combined with the opportunity to build a startup and access early-stage funding.

Who Is Alpha Looking For?

Alpha is looking for people who are highly technical and have demonstrated that they can build.

The programme specifically targets:

  • Highly technical software engineers
  • Exceptional students
  • Recent graduates
  • Recent graduates within approximately three years of leaving school
  • People with a track record of building
  • Individuals with strong technical curiosity
  • People who want to move quickly into startups or entrepreneurship

The programme is not designed as a general graduate fellowship for applicants from every professional background.

It is specifically focused on software engineering talent.

A Programme for Builders

A central theme of Alpha is building.

The programme is intended for people who do not simply want to learn about startups but want to participate directly in building products, companies and technology.

For applicants joining the Startup Track, this means becoming a full-time engineer at a rapidly growing company.

For Founder Track applicants, it means having the opportunity to begin building a company full-time.

This makes Alpha particularly relevant to technically skilled individuals who want their early careers to involve substantial hands-on work.

The Two Alpha Fellowship Tracks

Startup Track: Join a Fast-Growing Portfolio Company

The Startup Track is designed for technical students and recent graduates who want to gain experience inside a high-growth startup.

Successful candidates can take full-time engineering roles at fast-growing companies within the a16z portfolio.

The fellowship portion lasts approximately two months, but the employment opportunity continues beyond the fellowship.

What the Startup Track Provides

Participants can receive:

  • A full-time engineering position
  • Employment with a fast-growing portfolio company
  • Salary
  • Equity
  • An eight-week in-person fellowship experience
  • A kickoff retreat
  • Founder AMAs
  • Small-group dinners
  • Access to members of the a16z speedrun community
  • Exposure to engineers, founders and investors
  • Continued employment after the fellowship

The role is not simply an internship or temporary placement.

Fellows are hired directly by the matched company and continue in their full-time roles after the fellowship concludes.

How Startup Matching Works

The matching process is designed around mutual fit between candidates and participating companies.

Candidates and companies rank their preferences, after which matches are made.

If a candidate is matched with a company and accepts the opportunity, the fellow becomes an employee of that company.

This is an important distinction: fellows who join startups are not employees of a16z simply because the company is part of the a16z portfolio.

Instead, the successful fellow is hired directly by the participating company.

Founder Track: Start Your Own Company

The Founder Track is designed for technically strong individuals who want to become entrepreneurs.

Its most distinctive feature is that applicants do not necessarily need to have already established a conventional startup.

Alpha states that it is willing to back founders at an extremely early stage, including before they have:

  • A legal entity
  • A complete startup idea
  • A founding team

This makes the programme particularly interesting for technical builders who have the ambition to become founders but are still at the beginning of the process.

Apply as an Individual

Founder Track applicants apply individually.

If an applicant already knows who they want to build a company with, each potential founder should submit their own application and identify the person or people they intend to build with.

This means that an applicant does not need to wait until they have assembled a complete founding team before applying.

Founder Track Funding

The Founder Track provides significant early-stage financial support.

Accepted founders receive an initial:

$20,000 grant

The programme also makes available:

Up to $250,000 in total investment

This gives accepted founders capital to begin working full-time on their company.

The programme’s stated timeline explains that accepted founders receive their initial $20,000 grant and begin working full-time on their idea, with up to $250,000 in total investment available.

This is particularly significant because Alpha is willing to support founders at a stage when they may not yet have a traditional venture-backed startup.

Potential Access to a16z Speedrun

Alpha also provides a potential pathway into a16z speedrun, described by the programme as its flagship startup programme.

Once Alpha fellows complete the fellowship with a team and company formed, they receive priority consideration for a16z speedrun.

The programme states that speedrun can provide:

Up to $1 million in investment

For aspiring founders, this means Alpha can potentially serve as an early step in a larger startup-building and fundraising journey.

The pathway can therefore look like:

  1. Apply to Alpha as a technical builder.
  2. Join the Founder Track if selected.
  3. Receive initial funding.
  4. Build a team and company.
  5. Complete the Alpha fellowship.
  6. Receive priority consideration for a16z speedrun.
  7. Potentially access further investment through speedrun.

The Eight-Week In-Person Fellowship

Both tracks include an approximately two-month, eight-week fellowship experience.

The programme is conducted in person and is designed to surround fellows with experienced technical and startup leaders.

The fellowship includes:

  • An immersive kickoff retreat
  • Curated dinners
  • Founder AMAs
  • Small-group discussions
  • Conversations with engineering leaders
  • Meetings with portfolio founders
  • Interactions with investors
  • Access to selected a16z speedrun events
  • Participation in the broader startup community

Rather than functioning solely as classroom-based training, the fellowship is designed around direct exposure to people building and funding technology companies.

Founder AMAs and Community Events

One of the programme’s notable features is access to founder conversations.

Fellows participate in founder AMAs, allowing them to learn directly from people who have built technology companies.

They also gain opportunities to participate in small-group dinners and discussions with people working across the startup ecosystem.

The objective is to give fellows exposure to the practical realities of building and scaling technology companies.

Speakers and Mentors

The Alpha Fellowship lists a range of technology founders, investors and leaders among its speakers and mentors.

These include:

Marc Andreessen

Marc Andreessen is listed as a co-founder and general partner at a16z.

Chris Best

Chris Best is listed as founder and CEO of Substack.

Michael Lingelbach

Michael Lingelbach is listed as founder and CEO of Hedra.

Lisha Li

Lisha Li is listed as founder of Rosebud AI and formerly of Pinterest.

Maxwell Wang

Maxwell Wang is listed as founder of Dispatcher and formerly of SpaceX.

Elena Wagenemas

Elena Wagenemas is listed as founder of Taya and formerly of Apple.

Andrew Chen

Andrew Chen is listed as a general partner at a16z.

Roland Fryer

Roland Fryer is listed as founding general partner at EO Ventures and a Harvard professor.

These connections provide fellows with exposure to experienced technology entrepreneurs, investors and operators.

Previous Speakers

The programme also highlights previous speakers associated with major technology companies.

These include:

  • Dylan Field, co-founder and CEO of Figma
  • Jeff Lawson, co-founder and CEO of Twilio
  • Adam D’Angelo, founder of Quora
  • Rahul Vohra, founder of Superhuman AI
  • Bobby Murphy, CTO of Snap
  • Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel
  • Kevin Weil, VP of OpenAI for Science
  • Emmett Shear, founder of Twitch

Fellows will also be invited to selected a16z speedrun events.

Career Opportunities Through the Startup Track

For early-career software engineers, the Startup Track offers more than a short-term fellowship.

The successful candidate receives a full-time role at a participating portfolio company.

This can provide experience in:

  • Product development
  • Software engineering
  • Startup environments
  • Rapid product iteration
  • Working with technical teams
  • Building products at high-growth companies
  • Collaborating with founders and operators

Because the role continues after the fellowship, fellows have the opportunity to build a longer-term career within their matched company.

Salary and Equity

Startup Track participants receive a full-time engineering position with:

  • Salary
  • Equity

Compensation is determined by the hiring company.

This means applicants should not assume that all fellows will receive an identical compensation package. The actual terms depend on the company and position into which they are matched.

The Founder Opportunity

For those who want to build rather than join an existing company, the Founder Track offers a different type of opportunity.

Instead of being matched to an established startup, the participant works full-time on creating a company.

The programme can support founders even before they have:

  • Incorporated a company
  • Developed a final product
  • Built a team
  • Fully defined the startup idea

This makes the Founder Track particularly relevant to technical people who have strong entrepreneurial ambitions.

Who Can Apply as a Student?

Students are eligible to apply.

However, the full-time nature of the programme is important.

Students selected for the Startup Track must be prepared to take on a full-time engineering position.

Founder Track participants are expected to work full-time on their company.

Therefore, students should consider whether they can make the required commitment before applying.

Recent Graduate Eligibility

Recent graduates can also apply.

The programme specifically focuses on recent graduates who are within approximately three years of leaving school.

This makes Alpha primarily an early-career opportunity rather than a programme for experienced engineers who have already spent many years in the industry.

Applicants should therefore consider how recently they completed their studies when assessing their eligibility.

U.S. Work Authorization Requirement

One of the most important requirements for prospective applicants is U.S. work authorization.

Applicants must have valid authorization to work full-time in the United States.

This requirement is especially important for international candidates.

Simply being a highly skilled software engineer or graduating from a university outside the United States does not remove the work authorization requirement.

Applicants who do not have the required U.S. work authorization should carefully review the official eligibility requirements before applying.

Geographic Eligibility

The programme information does not identify a specific race, nationality or continent as an eligibility category.

However, the U.S. work authorization requirement is a major practical eligibility condition.

The fellowship is also conducted in person, meaning successful candidates need to be able to participate physically in the programme and relocate near the relevant a16z office.

Consequently, prospective international applicants should evaluate both their work authorization and ability to relocate.

Is Alpha Only for Software Engineers?

Yes.

The programme states that Alpha is exclusively for software engineers.

It is therefore not intended as a general technology fellowship for every technical profession.

Applicants whose primary background is in areas such as:

  • Graphic design
  • Marketing
  • Communications
  • Sales
  • Finance
  • General business
  • Non-technical operations

should not assume that the programme is suitable for them unless they also meet the software engineering requirements.

What Does “Track Record of Building” Mean?

Alpha is looking for people who can demonstrate that they build.

For applicants, this could mean being able to show evidence of:

  • Software projects
  • Products
  • Applications
  • Technical experiments
  • Startup projects
  • Open-source work
  • Other substantial technical projects

The exact evidence will vary from applicant to applicant, but the underlying idea is that Alpha wants people who demonstrate initiative and technical execution.

For more information on Alpha Fellowship 2026, VISIT HERE.

How the Application Process Works

The Alpha Fellowship selection process has several stages.

Stage 1: Submit an Application

Applicants submit their application through the official Alpha application portal.

The programme encourages candidates to apply early.

The current programme information states that Cohort 1 applications have closed and that applicants can submit applications to be considered when Cohort 2 opens in September 2026.

Early applicants receive priority review.

Stage 2: Technical Assessment and Interviews

Selected applicants proceed to a technical assessment and live interviews.

This stage allows the programme to evaluate the applicant’s technical ability and overall fit.

Stage 3: Begin Full-Time

Successful candidates then proceed according to their selected track.

Startup Track

Candidates and companies rank preferences and matches are made according to mutual fit.

Successful candidates are hired directly by their matched company.

Founder Track

Accepted founders receive their initial $20,000 grant and begin working full-time on their startup idea.

They can potentially receive up to $250,000 in total investment.

Stage 4: The On-Ramp

The fellowship begins with an immersive retreat.

During the retreat, fellows meet one another and spend time with the a16z speedrun team.

Stage 5: Fellowship Programming

From the beginning of the fellowship through its completion, fellows participate in weekly small-group conversations with engineers, operators and investors.

These conversations take place alongside the fellows’ normal full-time work.

Stage 6: Completion

The fellowship concludes with a capstone event.

Fellows present to the a16z speedrun team and broader community.

Startup Track fellows continue working in their full-time positions after the fellowship.

Founder Track participants continue building their companies.

Fellowship Timeline

The programme information provides a six-step timeline:

01. Application

Submit an application and be considered for the relevant cohort.

02. Interview and Assessment

Complete the technical assessment and live interviews if selected.

03. Full-Time Start

Begin either the startup role or full-time company-building journey.

04. On-Ramp

Participate in the immersive kickoff retreat.

05. Fellowship Programming

Take part in weekly discussions, dinners and conversations with leaders from the technology and startup ecosystem.

06. Completion

Complete the fellowship through the capstone event and continue along the selected career or founder pathway.

Cohort 1 and Cohort 2 Application Status

Applicants should pay close attention to the cohort information.

The programme states that:

Cohort 1 applications have closed.

The application information directs candidates to submit applications for consideration when:

Cohort 2 opens in September 2026.

The programme also states that early applicants receive priority review.

This means applicants interested in Cohort 2 should not wait until the last possible moment.

Is There a Final Application Deadline?

The information provided does not give a specific final closing date for Cohort 2.

Instead, the website states that Cohort 2 opens in September 2026 and encourages applicants to apply early because early applicants receive priority review.

Therefore, prospective applicants should not invent or assume a September 30 deadline.

The safest approach is to monitor the official Alpha application page and apply as soon as the Cohort 2 application window becomes available.

How Many Fellows Will Be Selected?

The programme indicates that it may admit up to 10 fellows per track.

This means the programme could have up to approximately 10 participants in the Startup Track and up to approximately 10 in the Founder Track, although the exact number selected may vary.

Given the technical requirements and the benefits attached to both tracks, applicants should expect a competitive selection process.

Benefits of the Alpha Fellowship

The Alpha Fellowship combines professional experience, community, mentorship and potential financial support.

Key benefits include:

1. Full-Time Startup Employment

Startup Track fellows can receive full-time engineering positions at fast-growing portfolio companies.

2. Salary and Equity

Successful startup-track candidates receive salary and equity through their matched employer.

3. Startup Experience

Participants gain direct experience working in a fast-growing technology company.

4. Founder Opportunity

Technical builders can use the Founder Track to start their own company.

5. Initial $20,000 Grant

Accepted Founder Track participants receive an initial $20,000 grant.

6. Up to $250,000 in Investment

The Founder Track offers up to $250,000 in total investment.

7. Potential $1 Million Investment Pathway

Founder Track participants receive an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun, which can provide access to up to $1 million in investment.

8. Access to Experienced Founders

Fellows participate in conversations with technology founders, investors and engineering leaders.

9. Strong Startup Network

Participants gain access to the a16z speedrun and EO Ventures communities and events.

10. In-Person Community

The programme provides opportunities to build relationships with other technically strong builders in person.

Who Should Consider Applying?

The Alpha Fellowship may be especially relevant to a person who can say:

  • “I am a strong software engineer.”
  • “I have already built meaningful technical projects.”
  • “I am a current student or recent graduate.”
  • “I want to work at a high-growth startup.”
  • “I want to become a founder.”
  • “I want direct access to experienced founders and investors.”
  • “I am prepared to work full-time.”
  • “I have valid U.S. work authorization.”
  • “I can participate in an in-person programme.”

If these characteristics describe an applicant, Alpha may be worth serious consideration.

Who Is Less Likely to Be Eligible?

The programme is not designed for everyone.

Applicants may not be suitable if they:

  • Are not software engineers
  • Do not have strong technical skills
  • Have no evidence of building
  • Are not students or recent graduates within the relevant early-career window
  • Cannot work full-time in the United States
  • Cannot participate in person
  • Cannot relocate as required
  • Are seeking a part-time opportunity
  • Are specifically looking for a remote fellowship

Why Apply Early?

The programme explicitly encourages early applications.

According to the application timeline, early applicants receive priority review.

This is important because waiting until the end of the application period could put an applicant at a disadvantage compared with candidates who submit earlier.

Since Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026 and a specific closing date has not been provided, prospective applicants should prepare their materials in advance.

What Applicants Should Prepare

Although applicants should follow the official application requirements, candidates can prepare by gathering:

  1. An updated software engineering resume
  2. A clear record of technical projects
  3. Links or documentation demonstrating what they have built, where appropriate
  4. Information about educational background
  5. Evidence of technical achievements
  6. Details about startup or product-building experience
  7. A clear explanation of their career ambitions
  8. Their preferred pathway, where applicable
  9. Information regarding U.S. work authorization
  10. Availability for the full-time and in-person requirements

A strong application should make it easy for the selection team to understand what the candidate has built and why they are ready for an opportunity of this scale.

Application Link

Interested applicants can access the official application portal here:

APPLY HERE.

Because the programme encourages early applications and gives early applicants priority review, prospective candidates should avoid waiting until the last minute.

Key Details at a Glance

  • Programme: Alpha Fellowship
  • Focus: Early-career software engineering and startup building
  • Tracks: Startup Track and Founder Track
  • Target applicants: Highly technical students and recent graduates
  • Graduate window: Within approximately three years of leaving school
  • Technical field: Software engineering
  • Format: In person
  • Duration: Approximately two months / eight weeks
  • U.S. work authorization: Required
  • Startup Track: Full-time engineering role
  • Startup compensation: Salary and equity
  • Founder Track: Build your own startup
  • Initial Founder Track grant: $20,000
  • Potential Founder Track investment: Up to $250,000
  • a16z speedrun pathway: Automatic final interview
  • Potential speedrun investment: Up to $1 million
  • Estimated cohort size: Up to 10 fellows per track
  • Cohort 1: Applications closed
  • Cohort 2: Opens in September 2026
  • Early applications: Receive priority review
  • Final Cohort 2 deadline: Not specified in the provided information

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Alpha a fellowship, job or startup accelerator?

Alpha is structured as a fellowship with two distinct pathways. The Startup Track connects fellows to full-time jobs at portfolio companies, while the Founder Track supports participants who want to start their own companies.

Do I have to be a software engineer?

Yes. Alpha states that it is exclusively for software engineers.

Can current students apply?

Yes. Students are among the target applicants.

However, selected participants must be prepared to make the necessary full-time commitment.

Can recent graduates apply?

Yes. The programme is intended for recent graduates, generally within three years of leaving school.

Do I need a startup idea?

No, not for the Founder Track.

Alpha states that it can back founders before they have an entity, idea or team.

Can I apply with my co-founder?

You apply individually. If you already know who you want to build with, each person should apply separately and identify the person they intend to build with.

How much funding does the Founder Track provide?

Accepted founders receive an initial $20,000 grant and can have access to up to $250,000 in total investment.

Can founders receive more funding?

Founder Track participants receive an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun. The speedrun programme can provide up to $1 million in investment.

Will Startup Track fellows work for a16z?

No. Fellows are hired directly by the portfolio company they are matched with.

Is the programme online?

No. The fellowship is in person.

Do I need U.S. work authorization?

Yes. Applicants must have valid authorization to work full-time in the United States.

Is there a specific nationality requirement?

The provided information does not specify a nationality, race or continent restriction. However, the U.S. work authorization requirement applies.

When does Cohort 2 open?

Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026.

What is the application deadline?

A specific final deadline for Cohort 2 has not been provided. Early applicants receive priority review, so candidates are encouraged to apply early.

Conclusion

The Alpha Fellowship is designed for highly technical early-career software engineers who want to accelerate their path into the startup world.

The programme offers two very different but potentially powerful routes.

The Startup Track gives selected engineers an opportunity to join fast-growing portfolio companies in full-time engineering positions with salary and equity. The fellowship experience adds access to founders, investors, engineering leaders, retreats, dinners and the broader a16z speedrun community.

The Founder Track is aimed at technical builders who want to create something of their own. Rather than requiring an incorporated company, established team or fully developed startup idea, Alpha is willing to support founders at a very early stage. Accepted founders receive an initial $20,000 grant and can have access to up to $250,000 in total investment, while also receiving an automatic final interview for a16z speedrun, which can provide access to up to $1 million in investment.

However, prospective applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements. Alpha is specifically for software engineers, with a focus on exceptional students and recent graduates, generally within three years of leaving school. Applicants must have valid U.S. work authorization and be able to participate in the programme in person.

The application timeline also requires attention. Cohort 1 applications have closed, while Cohort 2 is scheduled to open in September 2026. A specific final deadline for Cohort 2 is not currently provided in the supplied information, but early applicants receive priority review.

For a technically strong student or recent graduate who wants to join a breakout startup or take the first serious step toward becoming a founder, the Alpha Fellowship could provide an unusually direct combination of employment, startup exposure, mentorship, community and potential investment.

Interested candidates should prepare early and monitor the official application page so they can apply as soon as Cohort 2 opens.

item.content:encoded:
Are you a university student, recent graduate, or aspiring technology professional looking for an opportunity to gain practical experience with a globally recognized technology company?

Cisco is offering internship and co-op opportunities across several countries and professional fields, providing students with the chance to gain hands-on experience, contribute to real-world projects, develop technical and professional skills, and work alongside experienced professionals.

Cisco’s official internship and co-op career platform currently features five internship opportunities across Norway, Poland, the United Kingdom, the United States and Vietnam.

The available positions span areas including software development, software engineering, finance, Internet measurement research and testing engineering, making the programme relevant to candidates with different academic and career interests.

Cisco explains that its internship programmes are designed to give participants exposure to real projects, opportunities for skill development and the chance to connect with industry leaders, stakeholders and peers. Its co-op opportunities are structured around students’ academic programmes, enabling them to gain meaningful work experience while developing professional expertise.

This makes Cisco internships an attractive option for students seeking to bridge the gap between classroom learning and professional employment.

About Cisco Internship and Co-op Opportunities

Cisco is a global technology company known for its work in networking, cybersecurity, collaboration, cloud technologies and other areas of digital infrastructure.

Its internship programme provides students with an opportunity to experience a professional technology environment while contributing to actual organizational projects.

Rather than being limited to observation or classroom-style training, Cisco describes its internships as opportunities involving hands-on exposure to real projects.

Participants can therefore gain experience in areas such as:

  • Software development.
  • Software engineering.
  • Network technologies.
  • Data analysis.
  • Artificial intelligence and machine learning.
  • Research.
  • Finance.
  • Engineering.
  • Hardware and software testing.
  • Supply chain operations.
  • Technology innovation.
  • Business operations.

The exact responsibilities depend on the individual internship.

The Cisco careers page currently indicates that there are five internship positions available, with the listings categorized under the broader internships, apprenticeships and co-op career area.

Current Cisco Internship Opportunities

The current Cisco internship page provides five opportunities across different countries and professional disciplines.

Below is a detailed overview of the positions listed on the page.

1. Software Development Intern — Krakow, Poland

Job ID: 2015133

The Software Development Intern position in Krakow, Poland is designed for students interested in software development and technology innovation.

The role involves joining a dynamic team and contributing to software-related projects.

According to the vacancy description, interns will support the design and development of technology platforms while working alongside experienced developers.

Key areas of the internship include:

  • Software development.
  • Technology platform development.
  • Software design.
  • Collaboration with experienced developers.
  • Participation in real-world technology projects.
  • Development of practical technical skills.

The position is identified as a hybrid opportunity.

Cisco describes this role as particularly suitable for final-year university students who are passionate about software innovation and interested in gaining hands-on professional experience.

For students preparing to transition from university into the technology sector, this type of experience can provide valuable exposure to professional software development practices.

Ideal candidates

Applicants interested in this position should have an academic or professional background relevant to:

  • Computer Science.
